1. The animation shows how inflation wears down what a fixed income can buy. Three illustrative retirees, Edna, Ruth and Carl, each start a 20-year retirement in a different period of US history: January 1949, August 2006 and January 1966. Each gets the same 2% annual raise. The label says it uses US consumer price (CPI-U) history, "not a forecast."

2. In frame 1, each person has a full row of crates, which stands for what their income buys. Over the 20 years, part of each row fades away. By year 20 (frames 3 to 6), Edna still has about 10 crates, Ruth has about 9, and Carl has only about 4.

3. The same 2% raise protects buying power very differently depending on how fast prices actually rose. Prices rose slowly for Edna's and Ruth's periods, so their raises nearly kept up. Carl's period (1966 onward) had high inflation, so his 2% raise fell far behind, and his income bought less than half of what it did at the start.

4. The animation doesn't state any advice. A viewer might take away that a fixed payout, or one with a small fixed raise, can lose a lot of purchasing power if inflation runs high. They might also conclude that the inflation environment during their own retirement matters a great deal.

5. The advice in answer 4 is my own conclusion. The animation only shows the crates shrinking and labels itself illustrative history, not a forecast. It doesn't mention annuities or recommend any choice.
